4. Equiv: Program Equivalence🔗

open scoped HasEval MyGetElem Com

4.1. Behavioral Equivaleence🔗

In an earlier chapter, we investigated the correctness of a very simple program transformation: the optimize_0plus function. The programming language we were considering was the first version of the language of arithmetic expressions -- with no variables -- so in that setting it was very easy to define what it means for a program transformation to be correct: it should always yield a program that evaluates to the same number as the original.

To talk about the correctness of program transformations for the full Imp language -- in particular, assignment -- we need to consider the role of mutable state and develop a more sophisticated notion of correctness, which we'll call behavioral equivalence.

For example:

  • X + 2 is behaviorally equivalent to 1 + X + 1

  • X - X is behaviorally equivalent to 0

  • (X - 1) + 1 is not behaviorally equivalent to X

4.1.1. Definitions🔗

For aexps and bexps with variables, the definition we want is clear: Two aexps or bexps are "behaviorally equivalent" if they evaluate to the same result in every state.

def Aexp.equiv (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : Prop := ∀ (st: State), a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st def Bexp.equiv (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : Prop := ∀ (st: State), b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st

Here are some simple examples of equivalences of arithmetic and boolean expressions.

example : Aexp.equiv (aexp { X - X }) (aexp { 0 }) := ⊢ aexp {X - X}.equiv (aexp {0}) st:State⊢ Aexp.eval st (aexp {X - X}) = Aexp.eval st (aexp {0}) All goals completed! 🐙 example : Bexp.equiv (bexp { X - X = 0 }) (bexp { true }) := ⊢ bexp {X - X = 0}.equiv (bexp {true}) st:State⊢ Bexp.eval st (bexp {X - X = 0}) = Bexp.eval st (bexp {true}) All goals completed! 🐙

For commands, the situation is a little more subtle. We can't simply say "two commands are behaviorally equivalent if they evaluate to the same ending state whenever they are started in the same initial state," because some commands, when run in some starting states, don't terminate in any final state at all!

What we need instead is this: two commands are behaviorally equivalent if, for any given starting state, they either (1) both diverge or else (2) both terminate in the same final state. A compact way to express this is "if the first one terminates in a particular state then so does the second, and vice versa."

def Com.equiv (c₁ c₂: Com) : Prop := ∀ (st st': State), (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st')

4.1.2. Simple Examples🔗

For examples of command equivalence, let's start by looking at a trivial equivalence involving skip.

theorem skip_left: ∀ c, Com.equiv (imp { skip; ~c }) c := ⊢ ∀ (c : Com), imp { skip; ~c }.equiv c c:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' ↔ st =[ c ]=> st' c:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' → st =[ c ]=> st'c:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ c ]=> st' → st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' c:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' → st =[ c ]=> st'c:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ c ]=> st' → st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' case mp c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c ]=> st' cases h with c:Comst:Statest':Statest'✝:Stateh1:st =[ ~(imp { skip }) ]=> st'✝h2:st'✝ =[ ~c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c ]=> st' cases h1 with c:Comst:Statest':Stateh2:st =[ ~c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙 case mpr c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { skip; ~c } ]=> st' c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~(imp { skip }) ]=> ?st'c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ ?st' =[ ~c ]=> st'c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ State c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~(imp { skip }) ]=> ?st' All goals completed! 🐙 c:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~c ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙

Similarly, here is a simple equivalence that optimises if commands.

theorem if_true_simple: ∀ c₁ c₂, Com.equiv (imp {if (true) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) c₁ := ⊢ ∀ (c₁ c₂ : Com), imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } }.equiv c₁ c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' ↔ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' → st =[ c₁ ]=> st'c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' → st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' → st =[ c₁ ]=> st'c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':State⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' → st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' case mp c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' cases h with c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Statehb✝:Bexp.eval st (bexp {true}) = truehc✝:st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙 c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Statehb✝:Bexp.eval st (bexp {true}) = falsehc✝:st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙 case mpr c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { if (true) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ Bexp.eval st (bexp {true}) = truec₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st' c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ Bexp.eval st (bexp {true}) = true All goals completed! 🐙 c₁:Comc₂:Comst:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙

Of course, no programmer would write a conditional whose condition is literally true. (At least, no human programmer -- compilers and macro preprocessors do this sort of thing internally all the time!) But they might write one whose condition is equivalent to true:

Theorem: If b is equivalent to true, then if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂} is equivalent to c₁. Proof:

  • (->) We must show, for all st and st', that if st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st' then st =[ c₁ ]=> st'.

    Proceed by cases on the rules that could possibly have been used to show st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st', namely Com.EvalR.ifTrue and Com.EvalR.ifFalse.

    • Suppose the final rule in the derivation of st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st' was Com.EvalR.ifTrue. We then have, by the premises of Com.EvalR.ifTrue, that st =[ c₁ ]=> st'. This is exactly what we set out to prove.

    • On the other hand, suppose the final rule in the derivation of st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st' was Com.EvalR.ifFalse. We then know that b.eval st = false and st =[ c₂ ]=> st'.

      Recall that b is equivalent to true, i.e., forall st, b.eval st = (bexp {true}).eval st. In particular, this means that b.eval st = true, since (bexp {true}).eval st = true. But this is a contradiction, since Com.EvalR.ifFalse requires that b.eval st = false. Thus, the final rule could not have been Com.EvalR.ifFalse.

  • (<-) We must show, for all st and st', that if st =[ c₁ ]=> st' then st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'.

    Since b is equivalent to true, we know that b.eval st = (bexp {true}).eval st = true = true. Together with the assumption that st =[ c₁ ]=> st', we can apply Com.EvalR.ifTrue to derive st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'.

Here is the formal version of this proof:

theorem if_true_equiv: ∀ b c₁ c₂, Bexp.equiv b (bexp {true}) -> Com.equiv (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) c₁ := ⊢ ∀ (b : Bexp) (c₁ c₂ : Com), b.equiv (bexp {true}) → imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } }.equiv c₁ b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' ↔ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' → st =[ c₁ ]=> st'b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' → st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' → st =[ c₁ ]=> st'b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' → st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' case mp b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' cases h with b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Statehb✝:Bexp.eval st b = truehc✝:st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙 b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Statehb':Bexp.eval st b = falsehc:st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:∀ (st : State), Bexp.eval st b = Bexp.eval st (bexp {true})st:Statest':Statehb':Bexp.eval st b = falsehc:st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st'; b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:∀ (st : State), Bexp.eval st b = truest:Statest':Statehb':Bexp.eval st b = falsehc:st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:∀ (st : State), Bexp.eval st b = truest:Statest':Statehb':true = falsehc:st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ c₁ ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙 case mpr b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } } ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ Bexp.eval st b = trueb:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st' b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ Bexp.eval st b = trueb:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st' try All goals completed! 🐙 b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:∀ (st : State), Bexp.eval st b = Bexp.eval st (bexp {true})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ Bexp.eval st b = true; b:Bexpc₁:Comc₂:Comhb:∀ (st : State), Bexp.eval st b = truest:Statest':Stateh:st =[ c₁ ]=> st'⊢ Bexp.eval st b = true All goals completed! theorem declaration uses `sorry`swap_if_branches : ∀ b c₁ c₂, Com.equiv (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) (imp {if (¬ ~b) {~c₂} else {~c₁}}) := ⊢ ∀ (b : Bexp) (c₁ c₂ : Com), imp { if (~b) { ~c₁ } else { ~c₂ } }.equiv (imp { if (¬ ~b) { ~c₂ } else { ~c₁ } }) All goals completed! 🐙

For while loops, we can give a similar pair of theorems. A loop whose guard is equivalent to false is equivalent to skip, while a loop whose guard is equivalent to true is equivalent to while (true) {skip;} end (or any other non-terminating program).

The first of these facts is easy.

theorem while_false_equiv : ∀ b c, Bexp.equiv b (bexp {false}) -> Com.equiv (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) (imp {skip}) := ⊢ ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com), b.equiv (bexp {false}) → imp { while (~b) { ~c } }.equiv (imp { skip }) b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' ↔ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st' b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st'b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st'b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' case mp b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st' cases h with b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statehb✝:Bexp.eval st b = false⊢ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st All goals completed! 🐙 b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':Statest'✝:Statehb':Bexp.eval st b = truehc:st =[ ~c ]=> st'✝hloop:st'✝ =[ ~(imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st' b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':Statest'✝:Statehb':Bexp.eval st (bexp {false}) = truehc:st =[ ~c ]=> st'✝hloop:st'✝ =[ ~(imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st' All goals completed! 🐙 case mpr b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:Statest':Stateh:st =[ imp { skip } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' cases h with b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:State⊢ st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st b:Bexpc:Comhb:b.equiv (bexp {false})st:State⊢ Bexp.eval st b = false All goals completed! 🐙
Exercise★★(while_false_informal) (Advanced, manually graded)

Write an informal proof of while_false_equiv.

To prove the second fact, we need an auxiliary lemma stating that while loops whose guards are equivalent to true never terminate.

Lemma: If b is equivalent to true, then it cannot be the case that st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'.

Proof: Suppose that st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'. We show, by induction on a derivation of st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st', that this assumption leads to a contradiction. The only two cases to consider are Com.EvalR.whileFalse and Com.EvalR.whileTrue; the others are contradictory.

  • Suppose st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' is proved using rule Com.EvalR.whileFalse. Then by assumption b.eval st = false. But this contradicts the assumption that b is equivalent to true.

  • Suppose st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' is proved using rule Com.EvalR.whileTrue. We must have:

    1. b.eval st = true, and

    2. there is some st₀ such that st =[ c ] => st₀ and st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'.

    3. Also, we are given an induction hypothesis saying that st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' leads to a contradiction,

    We obtain a contradiction by 2 and 3.

theorem while_true_nonterm : ∀ b c st st', Bexp.equiv b (bexp {true}) -> ¬ (st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st') := ⊢ ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State), b.equiv (bexp {true}) → ¬st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st' b:Bexpc:Comst:Statest':Statehb:b.equiv (bexp {true})contra:st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st'⊢ False b:Bexpc:Comst:Statest':Statehb:b.equiv (bexp {true})contra:st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st'key:∀ (c' : Com) (s s' : State), s =[ c' ]=> s' → c' = (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) → False⊢ False exact key (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st' contra (b:Bexpc:Comst:Statest':Statehb:b.equiv (bexp {true})contra:st =[ imp { while (~b) { ~c } } ]=> st'key:∀ (c' : Com) (s s' : State), s =[ c' ]=> s' → c' = (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) → False⊢ (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) = (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) All goals completed! 🐙)

A more interesting fact about while commands is that any number of copies of the body can be "unrolled" without changing meaning.

Loop unrolling is an important transformation in any real compiler, so its correctness is of more than just academic interest!

Proving program properties involving assignments is one place where the fact that we are treating equality on program states extensionally (e.g., x →ₜ m[x] ; m and m are equal maps) comes in handy.

4.2. Properties of Behavior Equivalence🔗

We next consider some fundamental properties of program equivalence.

4.2.1. Behavioral Equivalence is an Equivalence🔗

First, let's verify that the equivalences on Aexps, Bexps, and Coms really are equivalences -- ie, that they are reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. These proofs are all easy.

4.2.2. Behavioral Equivalence is a Congruence🔗

Less obviously, behavioral equivalence is also a congruence. That is, the equivalence of two subprograms implies the equivalence of the larger programs in which they are embedded:

aequiv a a' ------------------------- cequiv (x := a) (x := a')

cequiv c1 c1' cequiv c2 c2' -------------------------- cequiv (c1;c2) (c1';c2')

... and so on for the other forms of commands.

(Note that we are using the inference rule notation here not as part of an inductive definition, but simply to write down some valid implications in a readable format. We prove these implications below.)

We will see a concrete example of why these congruence properties are important in the following section (in the proof of fold_constants_com_sound), but the main idea is that they allow us to replace a small part of a large program with an equivalent small part and know that the whole large programs are equivalent without doing an explicit proof about the parts that didn't change -- i.e., the "proof burden" of a small change to a large program is proportional to the size of the change, not the program!

theorem Com.congruence.asgn : ∀ x a a', Aexp.equiv a a' -> Com.equiv (imp {x := ~a}) (imp {x := ~a'}) := ⊢ ∀ (x : Ident) (a a' : Aexp), a.equiv a' → imp { x := ~a }.equiv (imp { x := ~a' }) x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' ↔ st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st' x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st'x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st'x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st' → st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':Statehce:st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' case mp x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':Statehce:st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st' cases hce with x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Staten✝:Nath:Aexp.eval st a = n✝⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> x →ₜ n✝ ; st x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> x →ₜ Aexp.eval st a ; st; x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:State⊢ Aexp.eval st a' = Aexp.eval st a All goals completed! 🐙 case mpr x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Statest':Statehce:st =[ imp { x := ~a' } ]=> st'⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> st' cases hce with x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:Staten✝:Nath:Aexp.eval st a' = n✝⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> x →ₜ n✝ ; st x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:State⊢ st =[ imp { x := ~a } ]=> x →ₜ Aexp.eval st a' ; st; x:Identa:Aexpa':Aexpheqv:a.equiv a'st:State⊢ Aexp.eval st a = Aexp.eval st a' All goals completed! 🐙

The congruence property for loops is a little more interesting, since it requires induction.

Theorem: Equivalence is a congruence for while -- that is, if b is equivalent to b' and c is equivalent to c', then while (~b) {~c} is equivalent to while (~b') {~c'}.

Proof: Suppose b is equivalent to b' and c is equivalent to c'. We must show, for every st and st', that st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' iff st = while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'. We consider the two directions separately.

  • (->) We show that st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' implies st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st', by induction on a derivation of st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'. The only nontrivial cases are when the final rule in the derivation is Com.EvalR.whileFalse or Com.EvalR.whileTrue.

    • Com.EvalR.whileFalse: In this case, the form of the rule gives us beval st b = false and st = st'. But then, since b and b' are equivalent, we have beval st b' =false, and Com.EvalR.whileFalse applies, giving us st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st', as required.

    • Com.EvalR.whileTrue: The form of the rule now gives us beval st b = true, with st =[ c ]=> st'0 and st'0 =[ while {~b} {~c} ]=> st' for some state st'0, with the induction hypothesis st'0 =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'.

      Since c and c' are equivalent, we know that st =[ c']=> st'0. And since b and b' are equivalent, we have beval st b' = true. Now Com.EvalR.whileTrue applies, giving us st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st', as required.
